---
title: "Multilevel Network Meta-Regression IV: Estimands, Identifiability, and Generality"
---

## Introduction {#sec-mlnmr-est-intro}

Chapters 20 to 22 built an engine. Chapter 20 wrote the individual-level outcome model
(@def-individual-model) and proved the aggregation theorem (@thm-aggregation): the aggregate-level
likelihood is the individual model integrated over the within-study covariate distribution, and the
integration must be done on the response scale to avoid the Jensen aggregation bias
(@thm-aggregation-bias). Chapter 21 handled the discrete-outcome likelihoods that integration produces,
and Chapter 22 built the numerical machinery, Sobol' sequences, Sklar's theorem, and the Gaussian
copula, that evaluates the aggregation integral against a covariate distribution specified only by its
marginals and correlations (@thm-hypercube-integration). At the end of Chapter 22 we can fit a
multilevel network meta-regression (ML-NMR) to a network mixing individual patient data (IPD) and
aggregate data (AgD), and we can compute every integral the likelihood requires.

A fitted model is not yet an answer. Three questions stand between the likelihood and a usable indirect
comparison, and this chapter answers all three.

First, *which quantity, in which population?* A fitted ML-NMR model is a surface over covariate space:
the conditional mean outcome for each treatment at each covariate value. An indirect comparison is a
single number, a relative effect. To collapse the surface to a number we must average it over a
covariate distribution, and the choice of that distribution is a choice of *target population*. The
defining flexibility of ML-NMR is that this choice is free: we may report the relative effect in the
population of either trial, in a third decision-relevant population, or in any population whose
covariate distribution we can describe. The first half of @sec-mlnmr-est-estimand makes the resulting
**target-population estimand** precise, shows it is the ML-NMR realization of the transport g-formula of
Chapter 17 (@thm-target-population-estimand), and isolates the one place where the choice of population
genuinely bites: on a non-collapsible scale the marginal relative effect depends on the target's
absolute risk and on the spread of its covariates, not merely on their mean. This is catalogue result
H.20.

Second, *is the quantity even identified?* Flexibility is worthless if the data cannot pin down the
coefficients the estimand depends on. The estimand involves the effect-modifier interaction
coefficients, and an AgD study reports only a handful of aggregate means: too few equations, in general,
to recover a whole interaction vector. We prove that in the smallest useful network, one IPD trial and
one AgD trial, the shared effect modifier assumption (@def-sema) is exactly what restores
identifiability, and that without it the comparison is identified *only* in the comparator's own
population and nowhere else (@sec-mlnmr-est-2study, catalogue H.21). We then lift the result to larger
networks, where exchangeable or treatment-class structures on the interaction coefficients trade
strength of assumption for flexibility, and where the identification rests on network connectivity in
the precise graph-theoretic sense of Chapter 15 (@sec-mlnmr-est-large, catalogue H.22).

Third, *how does ML-NMR relate to everything before it?* We close with the generality theorem
(@sec-mlnmr-est-generality, catalogue H.23): ML-NMR contains, as exact special cases, standard network
meta-analysis and IPD network meta-regression, and it contains, as estimand-and-limit special cases, the
two population-adjustment methods of Part IV, matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated
treatment comparison (STC). The STC reduction is an exact functional identity: the ML-NMR aggregation
integral *is* the marginal STC predicted mean. The MAIC reduction is the coincidence of *probability limits* (the values two estimators settle on as the sample size grows) already familiar from the MAIC-STC equivalence (@thm-maic-stc-equivalence). Seen from the summit,
every method in Parts III and IV is ML-NMR with some piece switched off.

Throughout, $g$ is the link function on whose scale the model and effects are written, $\mathcal X$ is
the covariate space, and a population $\mathcal P$ is a distribution over $\mathcal X$ with density
$f_{\mathcal P}$; we abbreviate the target density $f_{\mathcal P^{*}}$ to $f_{*}$. We use the
relative-effect notation $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd): the marginal effect of
treatment $b$ versus treatment $a$ in population $\mathcal P$, on the stated scale. The ML-NMR
individual model and aggregate mean are those of Chapter 20; we recall them in @sec-mlnmr-est-setup.

## A running clinical decision problem {#sec-mlnmr-est-running}

Before any formulas, here is the decision this chapter serves. We return to it at every step and give it exact numbers in @exm-mlnmr-new-target.

::: {#exm-mlnmr-anticoagulant}
## The anticoagulant decision (the chapter's running example)
A health technology agency (say NICE) must decide whether to reimburse a new oral anticoagulant, treatment $A$, in preference to warfarin, treatment $B$, for patients at risk of stroke. The harm that matters is a major bleeding event, an *unfavorable* outcome. No head-to-head $A$-versus-$B$ trial exists. What exists is:

- an **individual patient data (IPD)** trial comparing $A$ against a shared comparator $C$ (a standard anticoagulant used as control in both trials), for which the analyst holds every patient's covariates and outcome; this trial enrolled a *younger, fitter* sample;
- an **aggregate data (AgD)** trial comparing warfarin $B$ against the same comparator $C$, for which the analyst holds only arm-level bleeding rates and a table of covariate summaries; this trial enrolled an *older, frailer* sample.

The one covariate we track is age, coded as a binary effect modifier $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $X=1$ for an older patient. Age is both *prognostic* (older patients bleed more regardless of drug) and an *effect modifier* (age changes how much each drug raises bleeding risk relative to $C$). The reimbursement population, a UK NHS target, is older and sicker than the IPD trial and need not match either trial exactly.

When we fit this network in @exm-mlnmr-new-target the estimated coefficients come out as follows: the drugs raise the bleeding log odds relative to $C$ by $\gamma_A=0.8$ and $\gamma_B=0.3$ at a younger patient, age carries a prognostic log-odds effect $\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4$, and, assuming (as @sec-mlnmr-est-2study justifies) that age modifies both drugs the same way, a single effect-modification slope $\boldsymbol\beta_2=0.5$. We carry these numbers through the chapter.

The decision maker does not want the effect of $A$ versus $B$ "in general." They want it *in their population*, on a scale they can act on: a bleeding log odds ratio, or a bleeding risk difference. That target-specific quantity is the **estimand** of this chapter. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What ML-NMR will do with this problem, in one breath.** Fit one conditional outcome model to both trials at once (the IPD patient by patient, the AgD trial through the aggregation integral of Chapter 20). This yields a *surface*: the predicted bleeding probability for each drug at each age. Then average that surface over the *target* population's age distribution to get a predicted bleeding probability per drug in that population, and finally contrast those predictions on the chosen scale. The three questions of this chapter are three questions about this decision. **Which quantity, in which population?** ML-NMR may average over the UK NHS age distribution, not only over a trial's. **Is it identified?** The AgD trial reports only two bleeding rates, so on its own it cannot recover how age modifies warfarin's effect; something must supply that, and the shared effect modifier assumption is the usual candidate. **How does it relate to earlier methods?** Switch off pieces of this one model and it becomes network meta-analysis, IPD meta-regression, MAIC, or STC. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The fitted model and its population-free surface {#sec-mlnmr-est-setup}

We recall the model and fix the one structural fact that makes target-population transport possible: the
ML-NMR coefficients other than the study baselines are *network-level*, shared across studies and hence
across populations.

::: {.remark}
**The ML-NMR model (recalled from Chapter 20).** A network of $J$ studies on $K$ treatments, with
treatment $1$ the reference, is modeled at the individual level (@def-individual-model) by the linear
predictor
$$
\eta_{jk}(x)\;=\;g\!\left(\theta_{jk}(x)\right)\;=\;\mu_j+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_k+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^\top x,
\qquad \gamma_1=0,\ \boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\mathbf 0,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-model}
for individual covariates $x\in\mathcal X$, study $j$, and arm $k$, where $\theta_{jk}(x)$ is the
conditional mean outcome, $\mu_j$ is the study-$j$ baseline, $\boldsymbol\beta_1\in\mathbb R^p$ the
prognostic main effects, $\gamma_k$ the treatment main effect of $k$ versus the reference, and
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\in\mathbb R^p$ the treatment-by-covariate interactions (the effect modifiers,
@def-effect-modifier). For an AgD arm the aggregate mean (@def-aggregate-model) is the response-scale
average
$$
\theta_{\bullet jk}\;=\;\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta_{jk}(x)\big)\,f_j(x)\,dx ,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean}
evaluated by the integration pipeline of Chapter 22 (@thm-hypercube-integration). The defining identity
@thm-aggregation packages @eq-mlnmr-est-model and @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean into one likelihood over the
combined IPD and AgD data, with parameter vector
$\boldsymbol\xi=\big(\{\mu_j\},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\},\{\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\}\big)$ (and any
dispersion parameters). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The symbols in @eq-mlnmr-est-model carry a lot of freight, so before using them we name each one in words in @tbl-mlnmr-params and, crucially, record whether it is *study-specific* (changes from trial to trial) or *network-level* (one value shared by the whole network). That distinction is the hinge of the chapter: only network-level quantities can be carried into a population where no trial was run.

| Symbol | Plain meaning | Scope | Role in transport |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mu_j$ | study-$j$ baseline: reference-arm outcome level in trial $j$ | study-specific | does not transport; a target needs its own $\mu_{*}$ |
| $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ | prognostic effect: covariate shift on outcome, any treatment | network-level | shared; shifts every arm equally, cancels in a conditional contrast |
| $\gamma_k$ | treatment main effect of $k$ versus the reference, at $x=0$ | network-level | shared; part of every relative effect |
| $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ | effect modification: covariate shift on treatment $k$'s relative effect | network-level | shared; the reason a relative effect can differ across populations |
| $\theta_{jk}(x)$ | conditional mean outcome (here a bleeding probability) at covariate $x$ | derived | the height of the fitted *surface* at $x$ |
| $g$ | link fixing the scale (logit, log, identity) | fixed | decides whether the baseline cancels from a marginal contrast |

: Reading the ML-NMR parameters. Study-specific means it changes from trial to trial; network-level means one value is shared across the whole network and can therefore be transported. {#tbl-mlnmr-params}

The coefficients $\boldsymbol\beta_1$, $\gamma_k$, and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ carry no study index:
they are common to the whole network. Only the baseline $\mu_j$ is study-specific. This is the modeling
assumption that lets a coefficient estimated where IPD is available speak about a population where it is
not, and it is worth recording as a lemma, because two different transport statements follow from it and
they behave very differently.

::: {#lem-mlnmr-surface-transport}
## The network surface is population-free; its relative-effect part is also baseline-free
Fix the network-level coefficients $(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\},\{\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\})$ of
@eq-mlnmr-est-model. For any population $\mathcal P$ with reference-arm baseline $\mu_{\mathcal P}$,
define the population-$\mathcal P$ arm-$t$ linear predictor and conditional mean
$$
\eta^{\mathcal P}_t(x)=\mu_{\mathcal P}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_t+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,t}^\top x,
\qquad
\mu_t^{\mathcal P}(x)=g^{-1}\!\big(\eta^{\mathcal P}_t(x)\big).
$$

1. **(Conditional relative effect is population-free.)** For any two treatments $a,b$ the conditional
contrast on the link scale does not depend on the population at all, neither on its baseline nor on its
covariate distribution:
$$
g\!\big(\mu_b^{\mathcal P}(x)\big)-g\!\big(\mu_a^{\mathcal P}(x)\big)
=\eta^{\mathcal P}_b(x)-\eta^{\mathcal P}_a(x)
=(\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})^\top x .
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-condcontrast}

2. **(Absolute arm surface needs the baseline.)** The arm-$t$ conditional mean $\mu_t^{\mathcal P}(x)$
depends on $\mathcal P$ only through its baseline $\mu_{\mathcal P}$; two populations with the same
baseline have identical arm surfaces, and two with different baselines have arm surfaces that differ by a
link-scale shift $\mu_{\mathcal P}-\mu_{\mathcal P'}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-mlnmr-est-model the link of the conditional mean is exactly the linear predictor,
$g(\mu_t^{\mathcal P}(x))=\eta^{\mathcal P}_t(x)$. Subtracting the two arm predictors, the common terms
$\mu_{\mathcal P}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ cancel, leaving
$(\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})^\top x$, which contains no
population-specific quantity; this is part 1. For part 2, $\eta^{\mathcal P}_t(x)$ contains
$\mu_{\mathcal P}$ additively and no other population-specific term, so
$\eta^{\mathcal P}_t(x)-\eta^{\mathcal P'}_t(x)=\mu_{\mathcal P}-\mu_{\mathcal P'}$ for every $x$ and
every arm $t$, and applying the fixed function $g^{-1}$ gives the stated shift. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The relative-effect formula transports across populations for free; the absolute risks do not. Part 1 says the *difference* between two arms on the link scale is a fixed function of covariates you may carry into any population, because everything population-specific (the baseline, the covariate distribution) sits equally in both arms and cancels. Part 2 says that to recover an *absolute* outcome level in a new population, say the bleeding probability on warfarin in the UK NHS, you must also know that population's baseline $\mu_{\mathcal P}$; the network coefficients alone cannot supply it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the asymmetry is the whole story.** Part 1 says ML-NMR builds in *conditional constancy of
relative effects* on the link scale (@def-conditional-constancy-relative): the conditional contrast
surface @eq-mlnmr-est-condcontrast is a fixed function of $x$, the same in every population, determined
entirely by the network-level $\gamma$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_2$. Part 2 says ML-NMR does *not* build in
conditional constancy of absolute effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute): an arm's absolute
outcome level in a target population requires that population's baseline $\mu_{\mathcal P}$, which is not
a network-level quantity. On a collapsible scale the baseline cancels out of any marginal relative
effect, so part 1 suffices; on a non-collapsible scale (@def-non-collapsibility) it does not, and the
baseline reappears. This single asymmetry drives the collapsibility dichotomy in @thm-target-population-integral,
the role of the anchor in @sec-mlnmr-est-generality, and the entire unanchored extension of Chapter 26.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Estimands in any target population {#sec-mlnmr-est-estimand}

::: {.remark}
**The stakes, before the definitions.** Here is what ML-NMR estimates, in words: for a named target population it predicts the mean outcome each treatment would produce in that population, then compares those predicted means on a chosen scale. On the identity scale the comparison is a risk difference or mean difference; on the logit scale, taken after averaging, it is a *marginal log odds ratio*. This is ML-NMR's advantage over the pairwise methods of Part IV: MAIC and STC report the effect only in the comparator trial's population, whereas ML-NMR reports it in *any* population whose covariate distribution you can describe. The price, made precise in @thm-target-population-integral below, is that on a non-collapsible scale (an odds ratio, a hazard ratio) you must *name the target population and supply its baseline risk* before the marginal number is even defined. Keep the anticoagulant decision (@exm-mlnmr-anticoagulant) in view: the quantity we are building is "the bleeding log odds ratio of $A$ versus $B$ in the UK NHS population," not "in general." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We now collapse the surface to a number. Fix a target population $\mathcal P^{*}$ with covariate density
$f_{*}$, and write the target arm mean
$$
\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P^{*})\;:=\;\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\eta^{\,*}_t(x)\big)\,f_{*}(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\eta^{\,*}_t(x)=\mu_{*}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_t+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,t}^\top x,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-armmean}
the response-scale average of the arm-$t$ conditional mean over $\mathcal P^{*}$, with $\mu_{*}$ the
target's reference-arm baseline. Equation @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean is @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean with the study
covariate density $f_j$ replaced by the target density $f_{*}$ and the study baseline $\mu_j$ replaced by
the target baseline $\mu_{*}$; it is computed by the very same Chapter 22 pipeline.

::: {#def-mlnmr-target-contrast}
## Target-population marginal and conditional contrasts
For treatments $a,b$ and target population $\mathcal P^{*}$, the **target marginal contrast** of $b$
versus $a$ on scale $g$ is
$$
\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})\;:=\;g\!\big(\bar\theta_b(\mathcal P^{*})\big)-g\!\big(\bar\theta_a(\mathcal P^{*})\big),
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-marg}
the difference of the link-transformed target arm means; this is the quantity denoted
$d_{ab(\mathcal P^{*})}$ in [Notation](/notation.qmd). The **target conditional contrast** of $b$ versus
$a$ is
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})\;:=\;\int_{\mathcal X}\Big[g\!\big(\mu_b^{*}(x)\big)-g\!\big(\mu_a^{*}(x)\big)\Big]f_{*}(x)\,dx,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-cond}
the target average of the conditional link-scale contrast, where $\mu_t^{*}(x)=g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t(x))$.
The order of operations distinguishes them: @eq-mlnmr-est-marg integrates *then* contrasts on the link
scale, while @eq-mlnmr-est-cond contrasts on the link scale *then* integrates. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the contrast subscripts (a warning).** By the convention of [Notation](/notation.qmd), $\Delta_{ab}$ is the effect of $b$ *versus* $a$: the second subscript is the treatment being evaluated, the first is the reference. Do not read the subscripts left to right. In the running example this matters constantly, so we tabulate it once in @tbl-mlnmr-contrast-key.

| Symbol | Reads as | In the anticoagulant example |
|---|---|---|
| $\Delta_{CA}(\mathcal P^{*})$ | $A$ versus $C$ | new drug versus comparator |
| $\Delta_{CB}(\mathcal P^{*})$ | $B$ versus $C$ | warfarin versus comparator |
| $\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})$ | $A$ versus $B$ | new drug versus warfarin (the decision) |

: The contrast $\Delta_{ab}$ always reads "$b$ versus $a$." {#tbl-mlnmr-contrast-key}
:::

::: {.remark}
**Integrate then contrast, versus contrast then integrate.** @def-mlnmr-target-contrast defines two numbers a reader can easily assume are the same. The *marginal* contrast @eq-mlnmr-est-marg averages each arm's outcome over the population *first* and contrasts the two averages *after*: it is what you get by comparing population-level event rates. The *conditional* contrast @eq-mlnmr-est-cond contrasts the two arms at each covariate value *first* and averages the per-patient contrasts *after*: it is the typical patient-level effect. On a directly collapsible scale these coincide; on a non-collapsible scale they are genuinely different quantities with different data requirements, which is why the distinction is worth naming before it bites in part (c). In the estimand language of ICH E9(R1) it is part of the population-level summary an analysis must define. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The main result of this section identifies these estimands, gives the integral form, exhibits when the two coincide and when they part, and pins down exactly which target inputs each one needs. It rests on one import from Chapter 17. The **transport g-formula** (@thm-target-population-estimand) said, in words: to get a treatment's mean outcome in a target population, average its *conditional* mean outcome function over the target's covariate distribution. ML-NMR supplies the one missing piece, the conditional mean function itself, as the fitted surface $\mu_t^{*}(x)=g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t(x))$; the theorem below is that substitution made explicit.

::: {#thm-target-population-integral}
## Target-population estimand by integrating the fitted model
Suppose the ML-NMR model @eq-mlnmr-est-model holds across the network with network-level coefficients
$(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\},\{\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\})$, and that these coefficients together with
the baseline $\mu_{*}$ of a target population $\mathcal P^{*}$ are identified (the identifiability
hypotheses are supplied by @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study and @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large).
Assume the model is correctly specified on the covariate support of $\mathcal P^{*}$ and that
$g^{-1}\circ\eta^{\,*}_t$ is $f_{*}$-integrable for each arm. Then:

**(a) Identification and integral form.** The target marginal contrast $\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$ and
the target conditional contrast $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$ are identified, and equal
the integral expressions @eq-mlnmr-est-marg and @eq-mlnmr-est-cond. They are the ML-NMR realization of
the transport g-formula estimands of @thm-target-population-estimand: @eq-mlnmr-est-marg is that
theorem's marginal estimand with reporting scale $h=g$ and conditional means $\mu_t^{*}=g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t)$,
and @eq-mlnmr-est-cond is its population-average conditional estimand.

**(b) The conditional contrast needs only the covariate mean.** Because the conditional link-scale contrast is affine in $x$, that is, linear in $x$ plus a constant (@lem-mlnmr-surface-transport, part 1; this is also the sense in which the "linear surface" condition of @sec-mlnmr-est-generality is meant),
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})
=(\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})^\top\bar x_{*},
\qquad \bar x_{*}=\int_{\mathcal X} x\,f_{*}(x)\,dx,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean}
so it depends on $\mathcal P^{*}$ only through the covariate mean $\bar x_{*}$, and not at all on the
baseline $\mu_{*}$ or on the prognostic effects $\boldsymbol\beta_1$.

**(c) Collapsibility dichotomy for the marginal contrast.** If $g$ is directly collapsible (the identity
scale, @thm-identity-link-exact, or more generally a scale on which marginalization commutes with the
contrast), then $\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$ and the
marginal contrast also depends on $\mathcal P^{*}$ only through $\bar x_{*}$. If $g$ is non-collapsible
(logit, log-hazard, @def-non-collapsibility), then in general
$\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})\neq\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$, and the marginal contrast
depends on the *whole* target distribution $f_{*}$ and on the target baseline $\mu_{*}$, not only on
$\bar x_{*}$.

**(d) Computation.** Each target arm mean @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean is computed by the integration pipeline
of @thm-hypercube-integration; the marginal contrast is one link-scale subtraction of two such integrals,
and the conditional contrast is read off from @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean.

(Corresponds to H.20 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
**(a).** By @lem-mlnmr-surface-transport the conditional mean functions $\mu_t^{*}(x)=g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t(x))$
are determined by the identified network coefficients and the identified baseline $\mu_{*}$; in
particular they are fixed functions of $x$ once the baseline is fixed, and are the correct conditional
means in $\mathcal P^{*}$ by the correct-specification hypothesis. @thm-target-population-estimand
identifies, for any fixed function $\varphi$ of $x$, the target expectation $\int\varphi(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx$
by the transport g-formula. Applying it to $\varphi=\mu_b^{*}$ and $\varphi=\mu_a^{*}$ yields the two
target arm means $\bar\theta_b(\mathcal P^{*})$ and $\bar\theta_a(\mathcal P^{*})$; transforming by $g$
and differencing gives @eq-mlnmr-est-marg, which is the marginal estimand of
@thm-target-population-estimand with $h=g$. Applying it instead to
$\varphi(x)=g(\mu_b^{*}(x))-g(\mu_a^{*}(x))$ yields @eq-mlnmr-est-cond, the population-average
conditional estimand. The integrability hypothesis makes the integrals finite, so both estimands are
well defined and identified.

**(b).** By @eq-mlnmr-est-condcontrast the integrand of @eq-mlnmr-est-cond is the affine function
$x\mapsto(\gamma_b-\gamma_a)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,b}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,a})^\top x$. Integrating an
affine function against $f_{*}$ replaces $x$ by its mean $\bar x_{*}$ (linearity of the integral),
giving @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean. The constant and the linear coefficient are the network-level
$\gamma$'s and $\boldsymbol\beta_2$'s; neither $\mu_{*}$ nor $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ appears, because they
canceled in @eq-mlnmr-est-condcontrast. (Intuitively, the prognostic effects and the baseline shift both arms by the same amount, so they leave every contrast unchanged.)

**(c).** *Collapsible case.* Direct collapsibility of $g$ means, by definition, that for every arm the
link of the marginal mean equals the marginal of the link applied to the conditional mean,
$g(\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P^{*}))=\int g(\mu_t^{*}(x))f_{*}(x)\,dx$. Subtracting the arm-$a$ identity from
the arm-$b$ identity gives $\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$, and
by part (b) this depends on $\mathcal P^{*}$ only through $\bar x_{*}$. On the identity scale the equality
$g(\bar\theta_t)=\int g(\mu_t^{*})f_{*}$ is exactly the exact-aggregation identity of
@thm-identity-link-exact (both sides equal $\eta^{\,*}_t(\bar x_{*})$). *Non-collapsible case.* When $g$
is non-collapsible, $g$ does not commute with the response-scale average: by @thm-aggregation-bias
applied to the strictly convex or strictly concave $g^{-1}$ on the support of $\eta^{\,*}_t(X)$, the
quantity $g(\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P^{*}))=g\big(\int g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t)f_{*}\big)$ differs from
$\int \eta^{\,*}_t(x)f_{*}(x)\,dx=\int g(\mu_t^{*}(x))f_{*}(x)\,dx$ whenever $\eta^{\,*}_t(X)$ is
non-degenerate under $f_{*}$. The two arm discrepancies do not cancel in general, so
$\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})\neq\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})$. (A careful reader will object that $g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}$, the inverse-logit $\operatorname{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$, is convex below its inflection and concave above, not globally convex. The argument needs only strict Jensen applied to *each arm separately*: $\operatorname{expit}$ is strictly nonlinear on every nondegenerate interval, so each arm's response-scale average is strictly displaced from the average of its linear predictor, and the two displacements differ because the two arms sit at different baselines and slopes. It is the difference of the two per-arm displacements, not any single global convexity, that keeps the marginal and conditional contrasts apart.) Moreover the arm mean
$\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P^{*})=\int g^{-1}(\mu_{*}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\gamma_t+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,t}^\top x)f_{*}(x)\,dx$
is a nonlinear functional of $f_{*}$ that involves the baseline $\mu_{*}$ and the prognostic effects
$\boldsymbol\beta_1$ inside the nonlinear $g^{-1}$, so it cannot be reduced to a function of $\bar x_{*}$
alone: it depends on the full distribution of $\eta^{\,*}_t(X)$, hence on the spread of $f_{*}$ and on
the level $\mu_{*}$. The worked example @exm-mlnmr-new-target exhibits both phenomena numerically.

**(d).** Immediate from @thm-hypercube-integration applied to each arm integral @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean,
and from @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean for the conditional contrast. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The superpower and its price.** Part (a) is what distinguishes ML-NMR from the pairwise
population-adjustment methods of Part IV. MAIC and STC, by construction, report the relative effect in
the *comparator* population, because that is the population whose moments they match or whose covariate
distribution they integrate over (@thm-anchored-maic-consistency, @thm-stc-consistency). ML-NMR reports
the relative effect in *any* population $\mathcal P^{*}$ for which $f_{*}$ can be described, by simply
changing the density in @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean. The price is parts (b) and (c): on a non-collapsible
scale the marginal estimand is genuinely population-specific even when the conditional contrast is not,
so one must *name the target population* and supply its baseline risk before the marginal number is
defined. This is not a defect of ML-NMR; it is the non-collapsibility of the scale (@def-non-collapsibility)
made operational, and it is the same warning that governs @thm-target-population-estimand(c) and the
unanchored theory of Chapter 26. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**No overlap is required, but specification is.** Unlike MAIC, whose reweighting cannot manufacture
information outside the IPD covariate hull and is therefore undefined when the target strays beyond it,
the integral @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean is a model-based extrapolation: $g^{-1}(\eta^{\,*}_t(\cdot))$ is
defined at every $x$, so $\mathcal P^{*}$ may place mass anywhere. The honesty cost is that, where
$\mathcal P^{*}$ extends beyond the covariate region the network actually observed, identification in
part (a) rests on the parametric form of @eq-mlnmr-est-model continuing to hold there, an assumption the
data cannot check. ML-NMR shares this regression-style robustness to lack of overlap, and its dependence
on correct specification, with STC; the contrast with MAIC's no-extrapolation theorem is the point of the
generality results in @sec-mlnmr-est-generality. Concretely, if the UK NHS target is frailer or older than any patient the IPD trial enrolled, MAIC would refuse to answer, since there is no one to up-weight, whereas ML-NMR will still answer by trusting @eq-mlnmr-est-model out where no data constrain it. That extrapolation is the single assumption a decision maker should challenge hardest, and the honest response is a sensitivity analysis: refit under a plausibly different interaction slope $\boldsymbol\beta_2$, or restrict the target to the covariate range the network actually observed, and report how far the target estimate moves. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Two practical tables collect what the theorem demands of an analyst. @tbl-mlnmr-scales reads part (c) across the common scales; @tbl-mlnmr-inputs reads the same result as a checklist of target inputs.

| Scale $g$ | Collapsible? | Marginal contrast is | Needs target baseline $\mu_{*}$? | Needs full $f_{*}$ or just $\bar x_{*}$? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| identity (risk difference) | yes | risk or mean difference | no | $\bar x_{*}$ only |
| log (risk ratio, rate ratio) | collapsible, not directly | marginal log risk or rate ratio | no: $e^{\mu_{*}}$ cancels | full $f_{*}$ if $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ differ, else nothing |
| logit (odds ratio) | no | marginal log odds ratio | yes | full $f_{*}$ |
| log-hazard (hazard ratio) | no | marginal log hazard ratio | yes | full $f_{*}$ |

: How @thm-target-population-integral reads on each scale. On the identity scale the target baseline cancels and only the covariate mean matters; on the log scale the baseline cancels but the whole target distribution enters under effect modification; on a non-collapsible scale the whole target distribution and its baseline risk enter. {#tbl-mlnmr-scales}

| Estimand | Target mean $\bar x_{*}$ | Full target distribution $f_{*}$ | Target baseline $\mu_{*}$ | Fitted interactions $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| conditional contrast (any scale) | required | not needed | not needed | required |
| marginal contrast, identity scale | required | not needed | not needed | required |
| marginal contrast, non-collapsible scale | subsumed | required | required | required |

: Inputs required to compute a target-population contrast. The blank baseline entries are what "the baseline cancels" means in practice. {#tbl-mlnmr-inputs}

::: {.remark}
**Where does the target baseline $\mu_{*}$ come from?** On a non-collapsible scale the marginal odds ratio is undefined until the target's absolute risk level is fixed, so a health researcher must ask where that number originates. It is not read off the network; it is supplied from outside: from the reference-arm event rate in a registry or cohort representative of the target, from national epidemiology, or from the comparator arm of a trial judged close to the target. When the target matches neither trial, $\mu_{*}$ is often best treated as a *scenario input*, varied across a plausible range with the target estimate reported as a function of it. The dependence is real, not a nuisance: two populations with the same covariate distribution but different baseline bleeding risk have genuinely different marginal odds ratios, so uncertainty in $\mu_{*}$ is part of the honest uncertainty in the answer. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Prognostic variables do matter for a marginal odds ratio.** It is tempting to reason "a purely prognostic variable does not modify the relative effect, so it is irrelevant to the treatment contrast." Part (b) shows this is exactly right for the *conditional* contrast: $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ cancels. It is false for the *marginal* contrast on a non-collapsible scale. There $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ and the baseline $\mu_{*}$ set where on the sigmoid each patient sits, hence how much marginalizing bends the average, so a purely prognostic variable distributed differently in the target still moves the marginal odds ratio through @thm-aggregation-bias. This is why @tbl-mlnmr-inputs asks for the full $f_{*}$, not only the effect-modifier means, on a non-collapsible scale. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The math behind a regulatory debate.** Part (c) is not an academic curiosity. ICH E9(R1) asks an analysis to define its estimand, including the population-level summary, and the estimand-based reading of health technology assessment in @chandler2026transport makes explicit whether the target effect is *marginal* (population-averaged) or *conditional* (patient-level), precisely because the two disagree on a non-collapsible scale and transport by different rules. A conditional log odds ratio under SEMA is a single number good for every population (@eq-mlnmr-est-2study-cond); a marginal odds ratio must be recomputed, with a baseline, for each target. @thm-target-population-integral is the theorem underneath that requirement. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A monotonicity lemma for aggregate means {#sec-mlnmr-est-monotone}

Before the identifiability theorems we isolate the elementary fact that makes an AgD study informative
about scalar parameters at all. An aggregate mean @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean is a smooth, strictly increasing
function of any additive shift of the linear predictor; hence one observed aggregate mean pins one scalar
shift. This is the workhorse of both @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study and @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large.

::: {#lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone}
## Strict monotonicity of an aggregate mean in a scalar shift
Let $g^{-1}:\mathbb R\to(\ell,u)$ be continuous and strictly increasing (as the inverse of any strictly
monotone link is), let $f$ be a probability density on $\mathcal X$, and let $h:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$
be measurable with $g^{-1}(c+h(\cdot))$ $f$-integrable for every $c$. Define
$$
\Theta(c)\;:=\;\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(c+h(x)\big)\,f(x)\,dx ,\qquad c\in\mathbb R .
$$
Then $\Theta$ is continuous and strictly increasing, hence injective. If
$g^{-1}(z)\to\ell$ as $z\to-\infty$ and $g^{-1}(z)\to u$ as $z\to+\infty$, then the range of $\Theta$ is
the open interval $(\ell,u)$. Consequently, for any observed value $\theta^{\mathrm{obs}}\in(\ell,u)$ the
equation $\Theta(c)=\theta^{\mathrm{obs}}$ has a unique solution $c$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*When the integrability hypothesis holds.* For a bounded inverse link (logit, probit, complementary
log-log) it is automatic. For the log link, $g^{-1}(c+h)=e^{\,c-c_0}g^{-1}(c_0+h)$, so integrability at one
$c_0$ gives it at every $c$; for the identity link it is integrability of $h$.

*Strict monotonicity.* Let $c_1<c_2$. For every $x$, strict monotonicity of $g^{-1}$ gives
$g^{-1}(c_1+h(x))<g^{-1}(c_2+h(x))$, a strict pointwise inequality. The difference
$\Theta(c_2)-\Theta(c_1)=\int[g^{-1}(c_2+h)-g^{-1}(c_1+h)]\,f\,dx$ is the integral of a strictly positive
function against a probability density, hence strictly positive. So $\Theta$ is strictly increasing,
therefore injective.

*Continuity and range.* As $c\to c'$, $g^{-1}(c+h(x))\to g^{-1}(c'+h(x))$ pointwise by continuity of
$g^{-1}$, and for $c$ in a bounded neighborhood of $c'$ the integrands are dominated by
$|g^{-1}(c'+1+h)|+|g^{-1}(c'-1+h)|$, which is integrable by hypothesis; dominated
convergence gives $\Theta(c)\to\Theta(c')$, so $\Theta$ is continuous. Under the stated limits, monotone
convergence gives $\Theta(c)\to\ell$ as $c\to-\infty$ and $\Theta(c)\to u$ as $c\to+\infty$; a continuous
strictly increasing function with these limits has range exactly $(\ell,u)$. Injectivity then makes the
solution of $\Theta(c)=\theta^{\mathrm{obs}}$ unique for any $\theta^{\mathrm{obs}}\in(\ell,u)$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the lemma buys, and its limit.** For the logit link, $g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}$ has range
$(0,1)$, so an observed aggregate event proportion in $(0,1)$ identifies one additive shift of the linear
predictor uniquely; for the log link, range $(0,\infty)$, an observed positive aggregate rate does the
same. The lemma identifies *one scalar*, an additive shift, per observed aggregate mean. It does not
identify a *vector* of interaction coefficients from a single aggregate mean, because changing
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ reshapes the integrand $x\mapsto x^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k})$
rather than shifting it by a constant, and many such reshapings give the same integral. This gap between
"one scalar per aggregate mean" and "a whole interaction vector" is precisely the obstruction that the
shared effect modifier assumption removes, which is the subject of the next section. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Identifiability in the two-study network {#sec-mlnmr-est-2study}

The smallest network in which an indirect comparison is interesting has one IPD trial and one AgD trial
sharing a common comparator. We prove that under the shared effect modifier assumption the target
contrast is identified for any target population, and that without it the comparison collapses to a
single population.

We use the canonical anchored triangle of Part IV, now with one side reporting IPD: an IPD trial on
treatments $\{A,C\}$ in population $\mathcal P_{AC}$, and an AgD trial on $\{B,C\}$ in population
$\mathcal P_{BC}$, with $C$ the reference. The model is @eq-mlnmr-est-model with $K=3$ treatments and
$J=2$ studies; the AgD trial reports the covariate distribution $f_{BC}$ (its marginals and
correlations, from which Chapter 22 reconstructs $f_{BC}$) and the aggregate arm means for $B$ and $C$.

Before the theorem, three plain-language pieces make it readable: a picture of the network, a ledger of what is known and unknown, and a statement of what the shared effect modifier assumption (SEMA) is doing.

@tbl-mlnmr-triangle lays out the anchored triangle. The two trials share the comparator $C$; the target of interest, $A$ versus $B$, is not measured directly but chained through $C$.

| | IPD trial | AgD trial |
|---|---|---|
| treatments | $A$ vs $C$ | $B$ vs $C$ |
| data held | every patient's age $x$ and outcome | arm bleeding rates; covariate summaries |
| population | $\mathcal P_{AC}$ (younger) | $\mathcal P_{BC}$ (older) |
| what it can identify | $\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2,\gamma_A,\mu_{AC}$ | $\mu_{BC},\gamma_B$ (two scalars) |

: The anchored triangle with one IPD side and one AgD side. The shared vertex is $C$; the indirect target $A$ versus $B$ is chained through it. {#tbl-mlnmr-triangle}

The ledger of unknowns against data is @tbl-mlnmr-ledger. The moral is visible in its last row: one aggregate mean fixes one scalar (the monotonicity lemma), so an AgD-only interaction *vector* is underdetermined unless something supplies it.

| Unknown | What would pin it | Available here? |
|---|---|---|
| $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ (prognostic slope) | individual covariate variation | yes, from IPD |
| $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ (effect modification) | individual arm-to-arm slope difference | yes, from IPD (one vector for both drugs under SEMA) |
| $\gamma_A,\mu_{AC}$ | IPD arm means | yes, from IPD |
| $\mu_{BC}$ (AgD baseline) | one AgD arm mean, via monotonicity | yes, one scalar from the $C$ arm |
| $\gamma_B$ (AgD treatment effect) | one AgD arm mean, via monotonicity | yes, one scalar from the $B$ arm |
| $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ if *not* shared | a whole vector from one AgD mean | no: underdetermined |

: The two-study ledger. The books balance only because SEMA sets the AgD trial's interaction to zero new unknowns. {#tbl-mlnmr-ledger}

**What SEMA means here, clinically and arithmetically.** SEMA (@def-sema) says age modifies the $A$-versus-$C$ bleeding effect by exactly the same amount as it modifies the $B$-versus-$C$ effect: one slope $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ for both, $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$. Clinically it is the claim that the mechanism by which age amplifies anticoagulant bleeding is a property of the drug class, not of one molecule. Arithmetically it is what lets the IPD trial, which sees age at the individual level, hand the interaction to the AgD trial, which cannot estimate it. Count the AgD trial's contribution: two new unknowns ($\mu_{BC}$ and $\gamma_B$) against two data points (its two arm means); SEMA keeps its interaction at zero new unknowns, so the count balances. Drop SEMA and the AgD trial owes a whole $p$-vector $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ against the same two data points, and identification fails (@prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary).

With that in hand the proof is three plain steps: (1) the IPD $A$-$C$ trial estimates the shared slopes $\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2$ and the effect $\gamma_A$; (2) the AgD $C$ arm's bleeding rate pins the AgD baseline $\mu_{BC}$, one scalar from one mean; (3) the AgD $B$ arm's rate pins $\gamma_B$. With all five quantities known, $A$ versus $B$ transports to any target by @thm-target-population-integral.

::: {#thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study}
## Two-study identifiability under the shared effect modifier assumption
Consider the two-study network above, modeled by @eq-mlnmr-est-model on a strictly monotone link $g$,
under the shared effect modifier assumption (@def-sema)
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}=:\boldsymbol\beta_2 .
$$
Suppose the IPD trial has full-rank design (both arms present, with covariate variation of rank $p$
within the trial, so the IPD-NMR identifiability conditions of @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability hold for the
$\{A,C\}$ sub-model), and the AgD arm means lie in the open range of $g^{-1}$. Then:

1. The network-level coefficients $(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\gamma_A,\boldsymbol\beta_2)$ and the IPD baseline
$\mu_{AC}$ are identified from the IPD likelihood; the AgD baseline $\mu_{BC}$ and the treatment effect
$\gamma_B$ are identified from the two AgD aggregate means.

2. Consequently, for any target population $\mathcal P^{*}$, the target conditional contrast of $A$
versus $B$ is identified and equals the population-free constant
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\gamma_A-\gamma_B ,
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-2study-cond}
and the target marginal contrast $\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})$ is identified by
@thm-target-population-integral, given the target covariate distribution $f_{*}$ and (on a
non-collapsible scale) a target baseline $\mu_{*}$.

(Corresponds to H.21 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
*Step 1 (IPD identifies the network coefficients).* Restricted to the IPD trial, @eq-mlnmr-est-model is
a generalized linear model on arms $A$ and $C$ with linear predictors
$\eta_C(x)=\mu_{AC}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ and
$\eta_A(x)=\mu_{AC}+\gamma_A+x^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)$. By the IPD-NMR
identifiability theorem @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability (catalogue D.12), full column rank of the within-trial
design and a strictly monotone link identify all coefficients: the $C$ arm identifies
$(\mu_{AC},\boldsymbol\beta_1)$, and the $A$ arm then identifies $(\gamma_A,\boldsymbol\beta_2)$ from the
arm-to-arm difference in intercept and in covariate slope. In particular the shared interaction vector
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$ is known from the IPD alone.

*Step 2 (AgD identifies its baseline).* Treat $\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2$ as known from
Step 1 and $f_{BC}$ as reconstructed from the reported moments (Chapter 22). The aggregate mean of the
AgD reference arm $C$ is
$$
\theta_{\bullet,BC,C}=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\mu_{BC}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1\big)f_{BC}(x)\,dx
=\Theta_C(\mu_{BC}),
$$
which is $\Theta$ of @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone with shift $c=\mu_{BC}$ and
$h(x)=x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$. Since the observed $\theta_{\bullet,BC,C}$ lies in the open range of
$g^{-1}$, the lemma gives a unique $\mu_{BC}$ solving $\Theta_C(\mu_{BC})=\theta_{\bullet,BC,C}$, so
$\mu_{BC}$ is identified.

*Step 3 (AgD identifies its treatment effect).* Now treat $\mu_{BC}$ as known from Step 2. The aggregate
mean of the AgD active arm $B$ is
$$
\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\mu_{BC}+\gamma_B+x^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)\big)f_{BC}(x)\,dx
=\Theta_B(\gamma_B),
$$
which is again $\Theta$ of @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone, now with shift $c=\gamma_B$ and
$h(x)=\mu_{BC}+x^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)$, all of $h$ known. The observed
$\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}$ lies in the range of $g^{-1}$, so the lemma gives a unique $\gamma_B$. Thus
$(\mu_{BC},\gamma_B)$ are identified, completing Step 1's list.

*Step 4 (the target contrast).* By @lem-mlnmr-surface-transport(1) and SEMA, the conditional link-scale
contrast of $A$ versus $B$ is
$(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})^\top x=\gamma_A-\gamma_B$, a constant;
averaging over any $f_{*}$ (@thm-target-population-integral(b)) leaves
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=\gamma_A-\gamma_B$, which is identified because $\gamma_A$
(Step 1) and $\gamma_B$ (Step 3) are. This is @eq-mlnmr-est-2study-cond. The target marginal contrast
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=g(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal P^{*}))-g(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal P^{*}))$ is a fixed
function of the identified coefficients, of $f_{*}$, and of the supplied $\mu_{*}$, hence identified by
@thm-target-population-integral. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why SEMA is doing the work.** The IPD trial identifies the *shared* interaction vector
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$ for free, because in the IPD trial the interaction is estimated at the individual
level (Step 1). The AgD trial then only has to supply two scalars, its baseline and its treatment
effect, and the monotonicity lemma extracts exactly two scalars from its two aggregate means (Steps 2
and 3). The accounting balances precisely because SEMA reduced the AgD trial's unknown interaction from a
$p$-vector to nothing new. Drop SEMA and the AgD trial must identify a $p$-vector
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ as well, from the same two aggregate means; the books no longer balance, as the
next proposition makes exact. This is the network-regression face of the identifiability result
@thm-shared-em-identifiability of Chapter 17. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The failure without SEMA is not a loss of precision but a genuine non-identification, and it is
selective: the comparison survives in the comparator's own population and is lost everywhere else. We
make this precise.

In plain terms, the obstruction is this: with age's effect on warfarin left free, many different age-by-warfarin interaction patterns reproduce the *same* single aggregate bleeding rate the AgD trial reports, yet they disagree about warfarin's effect in any *other* age mix. The proposition makes that exact. (Read "$p$-dimensional manifold" as a smooth $p$-parameter family of equally good solutions, the "implicit function theorem" as the guarantee that this family is smooth, and a "generic target" as all but exceptional target populations.)

::: {#prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary}
## Without SEMA the two-study contrast is identified only in the comparator population
In the two-study network of @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study, drop SEMA and let
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}\in\mathbb R^p$ be free ($p\ge 1$). Then the AgD likelihood constrains
$(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$ only through the single scalar equation
$\Theta_B(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})=\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}$, whose solution set is a
$p$-dimensional manifold. Along this manifold:

1. The aggregate $B$-arm mean in the comparator population $\mathcal P_{BC}$ is constant along the
manifold (it is the observed datum), so the marginal target contrast $\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P_{BC})$, with
the comparator's own baseline $\mu_{BC}$, is identified.

2. For a generic target $\mathcal P^{*}\neq\mathcal P_{BC}$ the marginal target contrast
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})$ is *not* constant along the manifold; hence it is not identified.

Concretely, for a single binary effect modifier $X\in\{0,1\}$ with $\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=q$, there exist two
parameter pairs $(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})\neq(\gamma_B',\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}')$ producing the
*identical* AgD data yet different conditional $A$-versus-$B$ contrasts at every target mean $\bar x_{*}$
except at most one.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $\mu_{BC}$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ identified from Steps 1 to 2 of @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study
(those steps do not use SEMA), the only AgD equation involving the $B$-arm interaction is
$$
\Theta_B(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})
=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\mu_{BC}+\gamma_B+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}^\top x\big)f_{BC}(x)\,dx
=\theta_{\bullet,BC,B},
$$
one scalar equation in the $(p+1)$ unknowns $(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$. The partial derivative of
$\Theta_B$ in $\gamma_B$ is strictly positive (@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone), so $\nabla\Theta_B\neq 0$
everywhere; by the implicit function theorem the level set $\{\Theta_B=\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}\}$ is a
smooth $p$-dimensional manifold. Statement 1 is immediate: $\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P_{BC})$ is, by the
anchored identity, a function of $\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}$, $\theta_{\bullet,BC,C}$, and the IPD-identified
quantities, none of which moves along the manifold.

For statement 2 and the binary construction, take $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$, $\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=q$, write
$\beta_1$ and $\beta_2:=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}$ as scalars, and abbreviate $s_0:=\mu_{BC}$ and $s_1:=\mu_{BC}+\beta_1$ (the $C$-arm linear predictors at $X=0$ and $X=1$). The AgD $B$-arm equation is
$$
(1-q)\,g^{-1}\!\big(s_0+\gamma_B\big)+q\,g^{-1}\!\big(s_1+\gamma_B+\beta_2\big)=\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}.
$$ {#eq-mlnmr-est-binary-agd}
This is one equation in the two unknowns $(\gamma_B,\beta_2)$. Pick any $\beta_2$; the left side is
strictly increasing and continuous in $\gamma_B$ with range equal to that of $g^{-1}$, so by
@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone there is a unique $\gamma_B(\beta_2)$ solving @eq-mlnmr-est-binary-agd. The
map $\beta_2\mapsto(\gamma_B(\beta_2),\beta_2)$ traces the one-dimensional solution manifold. Choose two
values $\beta_2\neq\beta_2'$ and their solved partners $\gamma_B,\gamma_B'$. Both pairs reproduce the
exact same AgD data (and the same IPD, untouched). But the conditional $A$-versus-$B$ contrast at a target
mean $\bar x_{*}$ is, by @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean, $(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+(\beta_{2,A}-\beta_2)\,\bar x_{*}$,
and the difference between the two pairs is
$$
\big(\gamma_B'-\gamma_B\big)+\big(\beta_2-\beta_2'\big)\,\bar x_{*}.
$$
This is an affine function of $\bar x_{*}$ with nonzero slope $\beta_2-\beta_2'$, so it vanishes for at
most one value of $\bar x_{*}$, and for every other target mean the two observationally identical pairs give
different conditional contrasts. That value is not $q$ in general: differentiating
@eq-mlnmr-est-binary-agd along the manifold gives $d\gamma_B/d\beta_2=-q\,\dot g_1/[(1-q)\dot g_0+q\dot g_1]$,
where $\dot g_0:=(g^{-1})'(s_0+\gamma_B)>0$ and $\dot g_1:=(g^{-1})'(s_1+\gamma_B+\beta_2)>0$, so the
infinitesimal version of the root is $q\,\dot g_1/[(1-q)\dot g_0+q\dot g_1]$, which equals $q$ only when
$\dot g_0=\dot g_1$, as on the identity link. On a nonlinear link, therefore, even the conditional contrast
at the AgD mix is unidentified; what the data pin in $\mathcal P_{BC}$ is the marginal contrast of
statement 1. For statement 2, the marginal $B$-arm mean in a target $\mathcal P^{*}$ with a different
covariate distribution integrates $g^{-1}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_B+(\beta_1+\beta_2)x)$ against a different law, so
it moves along the manifold for all but exceptional targets. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-mlnmr-sema-fail}
## Two interaction patterns, identical data, different transported answers
Attach numbers to the construction, using the coefficients of @exm-mlnmr-anticoagulant. On the logit scale take the shared prognostic slope $\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4$, the IPD-identified $A$ interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=0.5$ and $\gamma_A=0.8$, an AgD baseline $\mu_{BC}=0$, and the older AgD mix $q=\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=0.6$. Suppose the AgD $B$ arm reports a bleeding proportion $\theta_{\bullet,BC,B}=0.6909$.

Two very different warfarin-interaction hypotheses reproduce this datum exactly. The SEMA-consistent pair is $(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})=(0.3,\,0.5)$; the no-modification pair is $(\gamma_B',\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B}')=(0.5717,\,0)$. Check both:
$$
\begin{aligned}
0.4\,\operatorname{expit}(0.3)+0.6\,\operatorname{expit}(1.2)&=0.4(0.574443)+0.6(0.768525)=0.6909,\\
0.4\,\operatorname{expit}(0.5717)+0.6\,\operatorname{expit}(0.9717)&=0.4(0.639166)+0.6(0.725419)=0.6909.
\end{aligned}
$$
They are observationally identical in the AgD trial. Yet the conditional $A$-versus-$B$ log odds ratio they imply, $(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)+(\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})\bar x_{*}$ with the IPD-fixed $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,A}=0.5$, diverges as soon as the target differs from the AgD mix:

| target mean $\bar x_{*}$ | SEMA pair | no-modification pair |
|---|---|---|
| $0.6$ (the AgD mix) | $0.500$ | $0.528$ |
| $0.2$ (a younger target) | $0.500$ | $0.328$ |

: Same aggregate data, two transported answers. {#tbl-mlnmr-semafail}

The two conditional answers already differ at the AgD mix ($0.500$ versus $0.528$), because the data pin only the *marginal* $B$-arm bleeding rate in $\mathcal P_{BC}$, not a conditional contrast; they coincide only at $\bar x_{*}\approx 0.54$ and separate as the target moves away. What is identified is the marginal comparison in $\mathcal P_{BC}$ itself (@prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary, statement 1). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The geometry of the surviving comparison.** Without SEMA the AgD study pins exactly one functional of
$(\gamma_B,\boldsymbol\beta_{2,B})$, the aggregate $B$-arm mean in its own population, which is the
covariate-weighted combination matching $\mathcal P_{BC}$. The comparison is therefore identified at, and
only at, $\mathcal P_{BC}$; pushing the estimand to any other target requires re-weighting the
unidentified interaction and reopens the manifold. This is the regression mirror of the testability
analysis @prp-testable-untestable-constancy: a single AgD contrast just-identifies the model at its own
covariate mean and leaves SEMA both necessary for transport and beyond the reach of two-study data. The
practical reading is the standard one of @phillippo2016tsd18: SEMA must be defended by pharmacological
argument and sensitivity analysis, not extracted from a two-study network. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Identifiability in larger networks {#sec-mlnmr-est-large}

With three or more studies the rigid SEMA constraint can be relaxed. We state and prove the general
identifiability theorem first under the shared-EM constraint, where a clean rank argument applies, then
record the exchangeable and treatment-class variants, which weaken the constraint at the cost of moving
from classical to Bayesian identifiability.

Throughout, the network has $J\ge 3$ studies, some IPD and some AgD, on $K$ treatments with reference
$1$, modeled by @eq-mlnmr-est-model. Recall from Chapter 15 the graph-theoretic notion of a connected
network: form the graph whose vertices are treatments and whose edges join two treatments compared
within some study; the network is *connected* when this graph is connected, equivalently when its
incidence matrix has rank $K-1$ (@thm-fe-nma-identifiability, catalogue D.8).

It helps to count once before the general statement. Take the smallest connected three-study network: $J=3$ studies on $K=3$ treatments (reference $1$), one IPD study on $\{1,2\}$ and AgD studies on $\{1,3\}$ and $\{2,3\}$, a single covariate ($p=1$), shared EM. The unknowns are three baselines $\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3$, two treatment effects $\gamma_2,\gamma_3$, one prognostic slope $\beta_1$, and one interaction $\beta_2$: eight scalars. The data reach them as follows. The IPD study identifies $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ (individual covariate variation) and its two cell intercepts. Each AgD arm mean pins one more cell intercept by monotonicity. The treatment graph has edges $12,13,23$ and is connected, so the identified cell intercepts $s_{jk}=\mu_j+\gamma_k$ separate into baselines and treatment effects exactly as in fixed-effects NMA. Every scalar is reached. The theorem is this accounting at scale, with the honest caveat that once interactions are allowed to differ by treatment (parts 2 and 3) the "IPD identifies the interaction" step must be re-earned class by class, or replaced by a prior.

::: {#thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large}
## Large-network identifiability under structured effect modification
Suppose the network is connected, the link is strictly monotone, and each study contributes at least one
observed arm whose mean (individual or aggregate) lies in the range of $g^{-1}$. Suppose further that the
IPD studies collectively identify the network covariate coefficients, in the precise sense that the
pooled IPD design satisfies the IPD-NMR rank conditions of @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability for
$\boldsymbol\beta_1$ and for the effect-modifier structure below. Then the full parameter vector is
identified under any of the following structural assumptions on the interactions.

1. **(Shared EM.)** $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_2$ for all $k\ge 2$ (one interaction
vector). The parameters $(\{\mu_j\},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 2},\boldsymbol\beta_2)$ are
classically identified.

2. **(Treatment-class EM.)** The active treatments are partitioned into classes
$\mathcal C_1,\dots,\mathcal C_m$, with $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_2^{(c)}$ for all $k$ in
class $c$; the parameters are classically identified provided each class contains at least one treatment
whose interaction is identified at the IPD level.

3. **(Exchangeable EM.)** $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}+\mathbf b_k$ with
$\mathbf b_k\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$ exchangeable across $k$ (@def-random-effects,
@def-exchangeability). Under a proper prior on the hyperparameters
$(\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}},\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$ and on the random effects, the model is
identified in the Bayesian sense (proper posterior), with $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$ and the
remaining parameters likelihood-identified as in part 1 and each $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ identified up to
partial-pooling shrinkage.

(Corresponds to H.22 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
**Part 1 (shared EM).** Under the shared constraint the free parameters are the $J$ baselines
$\{\mu_j\}$, the prognostic vector $\boldsymbol\beta_1\in\mathbb R^p$, the $K-1$ treatment effects
$\{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge2}$, and the single interaction vector $\boldsymbol\beta_2\in\mathbb R^p$. We identify
them in three blocks.

*Block (i): the network covariate coefficients $(\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2)$.* By hypothesis
the pooled IPD design satisfies the IPD-NMR conditions of @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability. In an IPD study
the linear predictor on a reference arm is $\mu_j+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ and on an active arm is
$\mu_j+\gamma_k+x^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2)$; with within-study covariate variation of
rank $p$ and at least one study carrying both a reference and an active arm, the individual-level GLM
identifies the common slope $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ (from any arm) and the shared interaction
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$ (from the slope difference between an active and the reference arm). These are
network-level, so once identified by the IPD they are known throughout.

*Block (ii): the per-arm intercepts $s_{jk}:=\mu_j+\gamma_k$ (the combined baseline-plus-treatment intercept of study $j$, arm $k$).* Treat $\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2$
as known from block (i). For each study $j$ and each present arm $k$, the observed mean of that arm
determines the scalar $s_{jk}$ uniquely: for an IPD arm, the individual-level intercept is identified by
the GLM; for an AgD arm, the aggregate mean is
$\theta_{\bullet jk}=\int g^{-1}(s_{jk}+x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top x\,\mathbf 1\{k\ge2\})f_j(x)\,dx
=\Theta_{jk}(s_{jk})$, a strictly increasing function of $s_{jk}$ by @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone, so
the observed $\theta_{\bullet jk}$ in the range of $g^{-1}$ pins $s_{jk}$ uniquely. Hence every present
cell's combined intercept $s_{jk}=\mu_j+\gamma_k$ is identified.

*Block (iii): separating baselines from treatment effects by connectivity.* The identified quantities
$\{s_{jk}=\mu_j+\gamma_k:(j,k)\text{ present}\}$ are the cell values of a two-way (study by treatment)
layout observed on the present cells. For two treatments $k,k'$ both present in study $j$, the within-study
difference $s_{jk}-s_{jk'}=\gamma_k-\gamma_{k'}$ is identified and is free of $\mu_j$. These within-study
treatment differences are exactly the edges of the network graph. Connectivity means the graph spans all
$K$ treatments, so the system of identified differences $\{\gamma_k-\gamma_{k'}\}$ over the edges
determines every $\gamma_k$ relative to the reference $\gamma_1=0$; this is the fixed-effects NMA
identification of @thm-fe-nma-identifiability, whose incidence matrix has rank $K-1$ precisely under
connectivity. With all $\gamma_k$ identified, each baseline follows from any present cell of its study,
$\mu_j=s_{jk}-\gamma_k$. Blocks (i) to (iii) identify the entire parameter vector.

**Part 2 (treatment-class EM).** Repeat block (i) within each class: by hypothesis each class
$\mathcal C_c$ contains a treatment whose interaction is identified at the IPD level, so the class
interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{(c)}$ is identified there, and $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ is identified from
any IPD arm. Blocks (ii) and (iii) are unchanged: the per-arm intercepts are pinned by monotonicity (now
using the class interaction appropriate to each arm), and connectivity separates baselines from
treatment effects exactly as before. The only new requirement, that each class carry IPD interaction
information, is the block analogue of the shared case's single requirement.

**Part 3 (exchangeable EM).** Now $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}+\mathbf b_k$
with $\mathbf b_k\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$ iid across active treatments, a
random-effects model (@def-random-effects) with the treatment-indexed interactions exchangeable
(@def-exchangeability). The likelihood, after integrating out the random effects $\{\mathbf b_k\}$,
depends on the hyperparameters $(\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}},\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$ and the fixed
parameters $(\{\mu_j\},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\})$. We argue Bayesian identifiability, the existence
of a proper posterior under a proper prior, together with likelihood-identification of the network-level
quantities.

The fixed parameters $(\{\mu_j\},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\{\gamma_k\})$ are identified by blocks (ii) and (iii)
of part 1, which used only the per-arm intercepts and connectivity and did not require the interactions
to be equal. The population interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$ plays the role of the shared
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$ in block (i): each treatment that carries IPD interaction information contributes an
identified treatment-specific $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$, and these are conditionally iid around
$\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$ with variance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_2$; their mean identifies
$\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$ and, when at least two treatments carry such information, their spread
identifies $\boldsymbol\Sigma_2$ (the normal-normal structure of @thm-conjugate-normal applied to the
identified interaction estimates). For a treatment carrying only AgD information, the single aggregate
equation underdetermines $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ exactly as in @prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary; the
random-effects prior regularizes it, and the posterior for $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is the proper
partial-pooling update, a precision-weighted compromise between the flat AgD information and the
hyperprior $\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}},\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$, in the manner of
@thm-conjugate-normal. With a proper prior on $(\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}},\boldsymbol\Sigma_2)$
and on the random effects, the joint posterior integrates to one (the likelihood is bounded and the prior
is proper, so their product has finite integral), which is Bayesian identifiability; and the
network-level quantities are likelihood-identified as stated. Two points make this weaker than parts 1 and 2. First, *bounded likelihood*: each individual or aggregate contribution is a probability or density evaluated at a mean in the open range of $g^{-1}$, and for the standard families (Bernoulli, Poisson, normal with bounded dispersion) this contribution is bounded above uniformly in the parameters, so the product likelihood is bounded on the whole noncompact parameter space and cannot by itself make an improper prior integrable. Second, *prior-identified versus likelihood-identified*: an AgD-only treatment's interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is not pinned by the likelihood at all, since its profile likelihood is flat along the manifold of @prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary; what determines its posterior is the hyperprior together with partial pooling toward $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$, and the data speak only through the treatments that carry IPD interaction information. That is the precise sense in which the exchangeable case buys flexibility with prior information rather than with data. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A ladder of assumptions.** The three structures form a ladder from strongest to weakest constraint.
Shared EM (part 1) imposes one interaction vector for the whole network and is classically identified by
a clean rank argument; it is appropriate when the treatments are pharmacologically alike. Treatment-class
EM (part 2) allows the interaction to differ across drug classes but not within them, classically
identified provided each class is anchored by IPD interaction information; it suits networks spanning
mechanistically distinct classes. Exchangeable EM (part 3) lets every treatment have its own interaction
while borrowing strength through a common distribution; it is identified only in the Bayesian sense,
because an AgD-only treatment's interaction is not pinned by the likelihood and survives only through the
prior. The honest summary is that flexibility in the interaction structure is paid for in assumption
strength and in reliance on the prior, and the choice should track network size and prior knowledge, as
@phillippo2019thesis recommends. The frequentist rank argument of parts 1 and 2 has no analogue for the
AgD-only interactions of part 3; this is a genuine limitation, not an oversight. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

@tbl-mlnmr-ladder summarizes the three structures and, importantly, what "identified" means for each.

| Structure | Constraint on interactions | Identification | When appropriate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shared EM | one $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ for the whole network | classical (rank argument) | treatments pharmacologically alike |
| Treatment-class EM | one $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{(c)}$ per drug class | classical, if each class carries IPD | mechanistically distinct classes |
| Exchangeable EM | each $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ its own, from a common distribution | Bayesian only (proper posterior) | many treatments, prior knowledge available |

: The ladder of effect-modification structures. "Classical" identification means the data alone pin the parameter; "Bayesian only" means an AgD-only interaction is pinned by the prior and by partial pooling toward the network mean, not by the likelihood. {#tbl-mlnmr-ladder}

::: {.remark}
**Where each hypothesis is spent.** Connectivity (the rank-$(K-1)$ incidence condition of
@thm-fe-nma-identifiability) is spent in block (iii) to separate the $\gamma_k$ from the $\mu_j$;
disconnect the network and a component of treatments floats free of the reference, exactly the NMA
failure mode of Chapter 15. The IPD interaction information is spent in block (i); remove it and
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$ (or $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{(c)}$, or $\boldsymbol\beta_2^{\mathrm{pop}}$) is
unidentified, the multi-study analogue of @prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary. The monotonicity lemma is spent in
block (ii); it is what lets an AgD arm contribute its one scalar intercept. Each "at least one observed
arm per study" assumption ensures every baseline is touched by some cell. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## ML-NMR contains NMA, IPD-NMR, MAIC, and STC {#sec-mlnmr-est-generality}

We close with the result that organizes Parts III to V: every earlier synthesis and adjustment method is
ML-NMR with a component removed. Two of the reductions are exact at the level of the model and likelihood
(network meta-analysis and IPD network meta-regression); two are reductions of estimand and probability
limit, with exact estimator coincidence in the linear case (MAIC and STC).

@tbl-mlnmr-roadmap is the map the theorem proves: each earlier method is this one model with a piece switched off. Read it before the formal statement.

| Method | What is switched off or restricted | The aggregation integral @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean | Resulting estimand | Data used to fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ML-NMR (full) | nothing | evaluated on the response scale | contrast in *any* target $\mathcal P^{*}$ | IPD patients plus AgD outcomes and moments |
| Standard NMA | $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0$ | collapses to $g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)$; no integration | $\gamma_b-\gamma_a$, the same in every population | arm-level outcomes only |
| IPD-NMR | every study is IPD | never invoked; covariates observed | individual-level contrasts | all patients |
| STC | fit the surface on IPD only; fix target to $\mathcal P_{BC}$ | the same integral, over $f_{BC}$ | comparator-population contrast | IPD outcomes only |
| MAIC | weight IPD to the $\mathcal P_{BC}$ moments | replaced by moment matching | comparator-population contrast | IPD outcomes, reweighted |

: The generality theorem as a roadmap. NMA is the row where the integral *collapses* because the integrand is constant (both covariate terms are zero); IPD-NMR is the row where the integral is *never needed*; STC keeps the very same integral but fits and targets more narrowly; MAIC replaces the integral by moment matching. {#tbl-mlnmr-roadmap}

One line to carry away: ML-NMR and MAIC agree exactly when the conditional outcome mean is affine (linear plus constant) in the covariates, and where the mean is genuinely nonlinear, ML-NMR's explicit integration over the whole distribution beats MAIC's matching of a few moments. STC and ML-NMR share the identical standardization integral; they differ only in what data fit the surface (IPD alone for STC, IPD and AgD jointly for ML-NMR) and in which target is allowed (the comparator for STC, any described population for ML-NMR).

::: {#thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma}
## The generality theorem
The ML-NMR model @eq-mlnmr-est-model, its combined likelihood @thm-aggregation, and its
target-population estimand @thm-target-population-integral contain the following as special cases.

**(a) Standard network meta-analysis (exact).** Setting $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0$ for all $k$ reduces @eq-mlnmr-est-model to $g(\theta_{jk})=\mu_j+\gamma_k$,
the fixed-effects NMA model. The aggregation integral @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean becomes exact with no
integration, $\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)$, the combined likelihood reduces to the
standard NMA likelihood in $(\{\mu_j\},\{\gamma_k\})$, and the target contrast is the
population-independent network contrast $\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=\gamma_b-\gamma_a$ for every
$\mathcal P^{*}$. In the two-study network this contrast is the Bucher estimand, consistent by
@thm-bucher-unbiased; in larger networks it is the NMA estimand identified by @thm-fe-nma-identifiability.

**(b) IPD network meta-regression (exact).** If every study is IPD, every covariate $x_{ijk}$ is
observed, the aggregation integral is never invoked, and the combined likelihood reduces to the
IPD-NMR likelihood of @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability.

**(c) MAIC (estimand and limit).** In the anchored triangle of @sec-mlnmr-est-2study under SEMA, with
target $\mathcal P^{*}=\mathcal P_{BC}$ the comparator population, the ML-NMR target contrast
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P_{BC})$ and the anchored MAIC estimator target the *same* estimand
$d_{BA(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ (MAIC reports it in the orientation $d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}=-d_{BA(\mathcal P_{BC})}$);
on the identity link, under the affine-mean conditions of @thm-anchored-maic-consistency, the two
estimators have the same probability limit.

**(d) STC (exact functional identity).** The ML-NMR aggregation integral @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean, applied
to the IPD-fitted linear predictor and a target covariate distribution, is identically the marginal STC
predicted mean of @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased. Hence ML-NMR restricted to "fit the outcome surface on the
IPD study alone, integrate over the comparator distribution" reproduces marginal STC, consistent by
@thm-stc-consistency.

(Corresponds to H.23 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
**(a).** Substituting $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\mathbf 0$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\mathbf 0$ into
@eq-mlnmr-est-model gives $\eta_{jk}(x)=\mu_j+\gamma_k$, independent of $x$. The aggregation integral
@eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean integrates the constant $g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)$ against the probability density
$f_j$, returning the constant itself: $\theta_{\bullet jk}=g^{-1}(\mu_j+\gamma_k)$, with no covariate
distribution entering. The aggregate likelihood thus reduces to the usual arm-level NMA likelihood in the
baselines and treatment effects, and the IPD likelihood reduces likewise (the covariate terms vanish), so
the combined likelihood is the standard NMA likelihood. For the estimand, the target arm mean
@eq-mlnmr-est-armmean is $\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P^{*})=g^{-1}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_t)$ (again the integral of a
constant), so
$\Delta_{ab}(\mathcal P^{*})=g(g^{-1}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_b))-g(g^{-1}(\mu_{*}+\gamma_a))=\gamma_b-\gamma_a$,
free of $\mu_{*}$ and of $f_{*}$, hence the same in every population: with no effect modification the
contrast does not vary across populations, which is transitivity holding exactly. In the two-study
network this is the Bucher estimand $d_{BA}=\gamma_B-\gamma_A$ chained from the two arm contrasts, whose
estimator is unbiased under transitivity by @thm-bucher-unbiased; in larger connected networks it is the
NMA contrast identified by @thm-fe-nma-identifiability.

**(b).** If study $j$ is IPD then each individual's covariate $x_{ijk}$ is observed, so the individual
conditional likelihood $\pi_{\mathrm{Ind}}(y_{ijk}\mid g^{-1}(\eta_{jk}(x_{ijk})))$ is evaluated at the
known $x_{ijk}$ with no marginalization; this is the IPD term of @thm-aggregation, and the integral form
@eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean is simply not used. With every study IPD the combined likelihood is the product of
such individual terms over all studies, which is exactly the IPD-NMR likelihood whose parameters
@thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability identifies under the stated rank conditions.

**(c).** By @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study and @thm-target-population-integral, the ML-NMR estimand at
$\mathcal P^{*}=\mathcal P_{BC}$ is the identified marginal contrast
$\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P_{BC})=g(\bar\theta_A(\mathcal P_{BC}))-g(\bar\theta_B(\mathcal P_{BC}))$, where
$\bar\theta_t(\mathcal P_{BC})=\int g^{-1}(\eta^{BC}_t(x))f_{BC}(x)\,dx$ is the arm-$t$ mean integrated
over the comparator distribution. This is, by definition, the marginal $A$-versus-$B$ effect in
$\mathcal P_{BC}$, namely $d_{BA(\mathcal P_{BC})}$. The anchored MAIC estimator of
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency is consistent for the same target (in the orientation $d_{AB}=-d_{BA}$) under
its hypotheses (conditional constancy, balance of every imbalanced effect modifier, overlap). For the
coincidence of limits on the identity link, note that MAIC's arm mean is the weighted IPD average
$\hat\mu_t^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\sum_i w_i\mathbf 1\{T_i=t\}Y_i/\sum_i w_i\mathbf 1\{T_i=t\}$ whose probability
limit, under the affine-mean condition $\mu^{AC}_t(x)=a_t+\mathbf a_t^\top x$ of
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency, is $a_t+\mathbf a_t^\top\bar x_{BC}$ (weighted balance forces the weighted
covariate mean to $\bar x_{BC}$). ML-NMR's arm mean in $\mathcal P_{BC}$ is $\int\mu^{BC}_t(x)f_{BC}(x)\,dx$,
the same affine function evaluated at $\bar x_{BC}$ but with the comparator's baseline in place of the
index trial's. The baseline is common to both arms and cancels from the $A$-versus-$C$ difference, so the
two $A$-versus-$C$ contrasts have the same limit, and combining with the comparator contrast gives the same
limit for the two indirect estimators. This is the
weighting-versus-modeling coincidence already proved for MAIC and STC in @thm-maic-stc-equivalence,
restated here with ML-NMR's integral playing the role of STC's regression prediction. On a nonlinear
surface the two limits can differ: ML-NMR integrates the full distribution $f_{BC}$ while MAIC matches
only the moments it balances, so ML-NMR generalizes MAIC by replacing moment matching with explicit
integration.

**(d).** The marginal STC predicted mean for arm $k$ in a population $\mathcal P$ is, by
@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased, the standardization (g-computation) of the IPD-fitted conditional surface
