over that population's covariate distribution,
$$
\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}(\mathcal P)=\int_{\mathcal X} g^{-1}\!\big(\hat\eta_k(x)\big)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx,
$$
where $\hat\eta_k$ is the linear predictor fitted on the IPD study. The ML-NMR aggregate mean
@eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean for the same arm and the same covariate distribution is the identical integral
$\int g^{-1}(\eta_k(x))f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx$. The two expressions are the same functional of the surface
and the density; the only differences are upstream and downstream of this integral. Upstream: STC fits
$\hat\eta_k$ by maximum likelihood on the IPD study alone, whereas ML-NMR fits $\eta_k$ jointly across
the IPD and AgD studies through @thm-aggregation, so the AgD *outcomes* (not merely the AgD covariate
moments) inform the fit. Downstream: STC fixes $\mathcal P$ to the comparator, whereas ML-NMR allows any
target by @thm-target-population-integral, and ML-NMR evaluates the integral by the Sobol'-copula
pipeline of @thm-hypercube-integration against a reconstructed $f_{\mathcal P}$, whereas STC typically
uses a Monte Carlo average over a simulated comparator sample. Restricting ML-NMR to fit on the IPD alone
and to integrate over the comparator distribution removes both differences and recovers marginal STC
exactly; its consistency is then @thm-stc-consistency. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The summit view.** Read downward, @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma says ML-NMR is the maximally informative
model in this book: it uses individual covariates where they exist (the IPD terms), aggregate outcomes
and moments where they do not (the AgD terms and the copula reconstruction), treatment-by-covariate
interactions (the $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$), and the full network structure (connectivity). Switch off
the covariate effects and it is NMA (a); give it IPD everywhere and it is IPD-NMR (b); restrict it to a
two-study anchored triangle reporting in the comparator population and it agrees with MAIC (c) and STC
(d). It never *loses* information relative to a special case, which is the formal justification, made
precise by parts (a) to (d), for taking ML-NMR as the default whenever IPD and AgD coexist. The two
adjustments it generalizes correspond to its two computational ingredients: MAIC is the weighting shadow
of integrating over the comparator's covariate mean, and STC is the regression shadow of integrating the
fitted surface; ML-NMR keeps both, the joint outcome model and the explicit integration, and adds the
freedom to choose the target population. The unanchored extension of Chapter 26 removes the anchor from
this picture, at the cost of the stronger absolute-constancy assumptions catalogued in
@thm-unanchored-maic-consistency. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A worked target-population estimate {#sec-mlnmr-est-example}

We carry a complete target-population calculation from a fitted ML-NMR model to relative effects in two
different target populations, choosing a single binary effect modifier so that every integral is a
two-term sum and every number can be checked with a calculator. The example exhibits, concretely, the
three phenomena of @thm-target-population-integral: integration over a target covariate distribution
(part a), the conditional contrast depending only on the covariate mean (part b), and the marginal
contrast on a non-collapsible scale being genuinely population-specific (part c).

::: {#exm-mlnmr-new-target}
## Population-adjusted estimates in two target populations
A connected network with an IPD trial on $\{A,C\}$ and an AgD trial on $\{B,C\}$ has been fitted under
SEMA on the logit scale, with a single binary effect modifier $X\in\{0,1\}$. This is the anticoagulant network of @exm-mlnmr-anticoagulant: $A$ the new oral anticoagulant, $B$ warfarin, $C$ the shared comparator, the event a major bleed, and $X=1$ an older patient. Throughout, $\operatorname{expit}(z)=1/(1+e^{-z})$ is the inverse-logit, so $\operatorname{expit}(\eta)$ is the modeled bleeding probability at linear predictor $\eta$. The fitted network-level
coefficients (treated as exact for transparency, as in the worked examples of Chapters 18 and 19) are
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_1=0.4,\quad \boldsymbol\beta_2=0.5,\quad \gamma_A=0.8,\quad \gamma_B=0.3,\quad \gamma_C=0,
$$
so the arm linear predictors in a population with reference baseline $\mu_{*}$ are, by @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean,
$$
\eta_C(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x,\quad
\eta_A(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x+0.8+0.5x,\quad
\eta_B(x)=\mu_{*}+0.4x+0.3+0.5x.
$$
The outcome is unfavorable (the event is bad), so on the logit scale a larger value of an
active-versus-$C$ contrast means the active treatment raises the odds of the bad event relative to $C$.

**Target $\mathcal P^{*}$: $\Pr(X=1)=0.6$, baseline $\mu_{*}=-0.5$.** The linear predictors and their
inverse-logits at the two covariate values are
$$
\begin{array}{llll}
\eta_C(0)=-0.5, & \operatorname{expit}=0.377541; & \eta_C(1)=-0.1, & \operatorname{expit}=0.475021;\\
\eta_A(0)=\ \ 0.3, & \operatorname{expit}=0.574443; & \eta_A(1)=\ \ 1.2, & \operatorname{expit}=0.768525;\\
\eta_B(0)=-0.2, & \operatorname{expit}=0.450166; & \eta_B(1)=\ \ 0.7, & \operatorname{expit}=0.668188.
\end{array}
$$
The target arm means @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean are the $0.4/0.6$ weighted averages over $X$:
$$
\bar\theta_C=0.4(0.377541)+0.6(0.475021)=0.436029,
$$
$$
\bar\theta_A=0.4(0.574443)+0.6(0.768525)=0.690892,\qquad
\bar\theta_B=0.4(0.450166)+0.6(0.668188)=0.580979.
$$
Their logits are $g(\bar\theta_C)=-0.257295$, $g(\bar\theta_A)=0.804292$, $g(\bar\theta_B)=0.326794$, so
the target *marginal* contrasts @eq-mlnmr-est-marg are
$$
\Delta_{CA}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.804292-(-0.257295)=1.061587\quad(A\text{ versus }C),
$$
$$
\Delta_{CB}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.326794-(-0.257295)=0.584089\quad(B\text{ versus }C),
$$
$$
\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=0.804292-0.326794=0.477498\quad(A\text{ versus }B).
$$
The anchored identity holds exactly: $\Delta_{CA}-\Delta_{CB}=1.061587-0.584089=0.477498=\Delta_{BA}$,
confirming that the $A$-versus-$B$ marginal effect is the difference of the two active-versus-$C$ marginal
effects in the *same* population, the network-consistency relation that licenses the indirect comparison. In words, in this older target (60 percent of patients in the older band) the model says the new drug $A$ raises the odds of a major bleed relative to $C$ by a marginal log odds ratio of $1.06$ (an odds ratio near $2.9$), warfarin $B$ raises them by $0.58$ (odds ratio near $1.8$), and $A$ versus $B$ is a marginal log odds ratio of $0.48$ (odds ratio near $1.6$): the new drug bleeds more than warfarin in this population.

**The conditional contrasts.** By @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean the population-average conditional contrasts on
the logit scale depend only on the covariate mean $\bar x_{*}=0.6$:
$$
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CA}=\gamma_A+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bar x_{*}=0.8+0.5(0.6)=1.1,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CB}=0.3+0.5(0.6)=0.6,\quad
\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}=\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5.
$$
The $A$-versus-$B$ conditional contrast is the SEMA constant $0.5$ of @eq-mlnmr-est-2study-cond, with the
interaction terms canceling. The marginal $A$-versus-$B$ effect $0.477498$ is smaller in magnitude than
the conditional $0.5$: a non-collapsibility gap of $0.022502$, the attenuation toward the null that
marginalizing a logistic model over a covariate produces (@def-non-collapsibility, @thm-aggregation-bias).
For the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast the gap is $1.1-1.061587=0.038413$.

**Target $\mathcal P^{**}$: $\Pr(X=1)=0.2$, same baseline $\mu_{*}=-0.5$.** The inverse-logits are
unchanged (the linear predictors do not depend on the population's covariate distribution); only the
averaging weights change, to $0.8/0.2$:
$$
\bar\theta_C=0.397037,\qquad \bar\theta_A=0.613259,\qquad \bar\theta_B=0.493770,
$$
with logits $-0.417828$, $0.461032$, $-0.024920$, giving marginal contrasts
$$
\Delta_{CA}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.878860,\qquad
\Delta_{CB}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.392908,\qquad
\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{**})=0.485952.
$$
The conditional contrasts move with the new mean $\bar x_{*}=0.2$:
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CA}=0.8+0.5(0.2)=0.9$ and $\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{CB}=0.3+0.5(0.2)=0.4$, while
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}=\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5$ as before.

**What the two targets show.** The $A$-versus-$C$ estimate is genuinely population-specific: its
conditional value moves from $1.1$ in $\mathcal P^{*}$ to $0.9$ in $\mathcal P^{**}$, and its marginal
value from $1.061587$ to $0.878860$, simply because the effect modifier $X$ has a different mean in the
two populations and $\boldsymbol\beta_2\neq 0$. This is effect modification transported: the same fitted
model gives different relative effects in different target populations, which is exactly the flexibility
of @thm-target-population-integral(a) that MAIC and STC, locked to the comparator population, do not
offer. The $A$-versus-$B$ conditional contrast, by contrast, is pinned at $\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5$ in
*both* populations by SEMA (@eq-mlnmr-est-2study-cond); yet its *marginal* value still drifts, from
$0.477498$ to $0.485952$, a residual population dependence that is pure non-collapsibility
(@thm-target-population-integral(c)): even with the conditional effect fixed, the marginal odds ratio
depends on the covariate spread and baseline risk of the target. A practitioner reporting a marginal odds
ratio must therefore name the target population; a practitioner reporting the conditional log odds ratio
under SEMA may quote the single number $0.5$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Baseline risk also matters, on a non-collapsible scale.** Repeating the $\mathcal P^{*}$ calculation
($\Pr(X=1)=0.6$) but with a high-risk baseline $\mu_{*}=1.0$ instead of $-0.5$ gives arm means
$\bar\theta_C=0.773734$, $\bar\theta_A=0.905476$, $\bar\theta_B=0.854484$, hence a marginal $A$-versus-$C$
contrast $\Delta_{CA}=1.030086$ and an $A$-versus-$C$ non-collapsibility gap of $1.1-1.030086=0.069914$,
nearly double the gap $0.038413$ at the low-risk baseline. The conditional contrast is $1.1$ in both,
unchanged by the baseline. This is the second half of @thm-target-population-integral(c): on a
non-collapsible scale the marginal estimand depends on the target baseline $\mu_{*}$, not only on the
covariate distribution, which is why producing a marginal target-population estimate requires the target
baseline risk as an input. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The same example on the identity scale (collapsibility in one line).** Rerun target $\mathcal P^{*}$ ($\Pr(X=1)=0.6$, $\mu_{*}=-0.5$) on the identity link, so $\theta_t(x)=\eta_t(x)$ and the contrast is a plain difference of means. The arm means are the weighted linear predictors $\bar\theta_C=0.4(-0.5)+0.6(-0.1)=-0.26$, $\bar\theta_A=0.4(0.3)+0.6(1.2)=0.84$, and $\bar\theta_B=0.4(-0.2)+0.6(0.7)=0.34$, so the marginal contrasts are $\Delta_{CA}=1.10$, $\Delta_{CB}=0.60$, $\Delta_{BA}=0.50$. These equal the conditional contrasts $\gamma_A+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bar x_{*}=1.10$, $0.60$, and $\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.50$ exactly: on a collapsible scale marginal and conditional coincide (@thm-target-population-integral(c)). The baseline $\mu_{*}$ has vanished from every contrast, because on the identity scale it is an additive shift common to both arms; changing it to $\mu_{*}=1.0$ leaves all three differences unchanged. Contrast this with the logit scale above, where the baseline did not cancel and the $A$-versus-$B$ marginal effect drifted with the population. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-mlnmr-est-notes}

Multilevel network meta-regression and all four results of this chapter are due to @phillippo2020mlnmr
and the thesis @phillippo2019thesis (Chapter 4 for the model, estimands, and identifiability; the
target-population estimand is §4.4, the two-study and large-network identifiability §4.5 and §4.6, and
the generality discussion §4.1 and §4.7). The chapter corresponds to results H.20 (the target-population
estimand integral, @thm-target-population-integral), H.21 (two-study identifiability under SEMA,
@thm-mlnmr-identifiability-2study), H.22 (large-network identifiability, @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large),
and H.23 (the generality theorem, @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma) of the proof catalogue in
`proofs/H_ml_nmr.md`.

The target-population estimand @thm-target-population-integral is the ML-NMR realization of the transport
g-formula estimands of Chapter 17 (@thm-target-population-estimand, catalogue E.12), which in turn rest on
the conditional-transportability theory of Chapter 12; the collapsibility dichotomy in part (c) is the
non-collapsibility of Chapter 7 (@def-non-collapsibility) made operational, the same phenomenon that
forces the marginal-versus-conditional choice in STC (Chapter 19) and that the worked example exhibits
numerically. Three arguments here go beyond @phillippo2019thesis. First, the statement that the AgD
trial identifies $\gamma_B$ through the aggregate likelihood is given a complete proof through the
monotonicity lemma @lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone, which isolates the
elementary fact (an aggregate mean is strictly increasing in any additive shift of the linear predictor)
that makes a single aggregate mean identify a single scalar; the same lemma then powers the large-network
argument. Second, the no-SEMA non-identification is stated as the proposition
@prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary, with an explicit binary-covariate two-point construction showing the comparison
survives in the comparator population and is lost at every other target, the regression mirror of the
testability analysis @prp-testable-untestable-constancy of Chapter 17. Third, the large-network theorem
@thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large is given a full block rank argument for the shared and treatment-class
cases (IPD identifies the interaction; monotonicity identifies the per-arm intercepts; connectivity, in
the incidence-rank sense of @thm-fe-nma-identifiability, separates baselines from treatment effects),
with the exchangeable case treated honestly as Bayesian identifiability via the normal-normal partial
pooling of @thm-conjugate-normal; the absence of a frequentist rank statement for AgD-only interactions
in the exchangeable case is recorded as a limitation, following @phillippo2019thesis §4.6.

The generality theorem @thm-mlnmr-generalizes-nma collects reductions to the fixed-effects NMA of
Chapter 15 (@thm-fe-nma-identifiability) and Bucher of Chapter 14 (@thm-bucher-unbiased), to the IPD-NMR
of Chapter 15 (@thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability), and to the population-adjustment methods of Part IV: MAIC
(@thm-anchored-maic-consistency) and STC (@thm-stc-consistency, @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased). The STC
reduction is the exact functional identity that the ML-NMR aggregation integral equals the marginal STC
predicted mean, so STC is ML-NMR with the outcome model fitted on the IPD alone and the target fixed to
the comparator; the MAIC reduction is the coincidence of probability limits under a linear surface,
already proved in another guise as the MAIC-STC equivalence @thm-maic-stc-equivalence. The complementary
fact that ML-NMR, like STC and unlike MAIC, does not require covariate overlap but does require correct
specification on the target support is the regression-versus-weighting trade-off of Chapter 19, and it is
why ML-NMR can report estimates in target populations that no single trial sampled. Ecological bias
(@def-ecological-bias, Chapter 16), the bias of naive meta-regression on study-level means, is exactly
what the response-scale integration of @eq-mlnmr-est-armmean avoids, by @thm-aggregation-bias.

ML-NMR has no counterpart in the companion Coq development: there is no `ML_NMR.v` (or aggregation or
network-meta-regression file) in `theories/`, because the substantive content of ML-NMR is numerical
(quasi-Monte Carlo integration, Sobol' sequences, copulas) rather than algebraic. Accordingly none of the results in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag; the
identifiability building blocks they invoke, the NMA and IPD-NMR rank theorems of Chapter 15, are
likewise pen-and-paper in this development. Chapter 30 discusses what is and is not in the Coq tree.

## Exercises {#sec-mlnmr-est-exercises}

Throughout, a $\star$ marks an exercise whose full solution appears in Appendix F. The exercises are labeled by type and roughly ordered from warm-up and interpretation through computation to proof and challenge; a beginner should manage the two warm-ups and @exr-mlnmr-third-target after one reading, while @exr-mlnmr-monotone-general and the starred exercises are proof-building challenges.

::: {#exr-mlnmr-which-population}
**Warm-up (interpretation). Which population, in words.** For the anticoagulant decision of @exm-mlnmr-anticoagulant, a NICE submission wants the effect of $A$ versus $B$ in the UK NHS population, which is older than the IPD trial and differs from the AgD trial too. State which population's covariate distribution ML-NMR should average the fitted surface over, and explain in one or two sentences why MAIC and STC, as defined in Part IV, cannot target that population directly. Which single extra input does a *marginal* odds ratio in that population require that a *conditional* log odds ratio does not?
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-inputs-checklist}
**Warm-up (reading the tables). What must you supply?** Using @tbl-mlnmr-scales and @tbl-mlnmr-inputs, list the target-population inputs needed to report each of: (i) a conditional log odds ratio; (ii) a marginal odds ratio; (iii) a risk difference on the identity scale. In each case say whether the target baseline risk $\mu_{*}$ is needed, and give the one-sentence reason (collapsible or not).
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-third-target}
**Computation. A third target by hand.** Continue @exm-mlnmr-new-target with a third target population having
$\Pr(X=1)=0.5$ and baseline $\mu_{*}=0$. Compute the six inverse-logit values, the three target arm means
$\bar\theta_A,\bar\theta_B,\bar\theta_C$, the three marginal contrasts $\Delta_{CA},\Delta_{CB},\Delta_{BA}$,
and verify the anchored identity $\Delta_{CA}-\Delta_{CB}=\Delta_{BA}$ to six decimals. Report the
conditional contrasts from @eq-mlnmr-est-cond-mean and the $A$-versus-$B$ non-collapsibility gap.
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-identity-link}
**Interpretation and computation. Collapsibility kills the population dependence.** Redo @exm-mlnmr-new-target on the identity link
(replace $\operatorname{expit}$ by the identity, so $\theta_t(x)=\eta_t(x)$), using the same coefficients
and the two targets $\mathcal P^{*}$ ($\Pr(X=1)=0.6$) and $\mathcal P^{**}$ ($\Pr(X=1)=0.2$). Show that
the marginal and conditional contrasts coincide, that the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast equals $\gamma_A-\gamma_B=0.5$
in *both* targets, and that the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast depends on the target only through $\bar x_{*}$.
Explain, by reference to @thm-identity-link-exact and @thm-target-population-integral(c), why the baseline
$\mu_{*}$ has now disappeared from every contrast.
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-monotone-general}
**Challenge (proof). Monotonicity with a tilt instead of a shift.** Replace the additive shift in
@lem-mlnmr-aggregate-monotone by a one-parameter family $c\mapsto\Theta_{\mathbf v}(c):=\int g^{-1}(c\,\mathbf v^\top x+h(x))f(x)\,dx$
that *tilts* the linear predictor along a fixed direction $\mathbf v$. Show that $\Theta_{\mathbf v}$ need
*not* be monotone in $c$, and exhibit a density $f$ on $\{0,1\}$ (or on a two-point support) and a
direction for which two values of $c$ give the same $\Theta_{\mathbf v}$. Explain how this
non-monotonicity is exactly the obstruction that defeats identification of a free interaction vector from
one aggregate mean, connecting to the manifold in @prp-mlnmr-sema-necessary.
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-network-rank}
**Computation. Counting in a three-study network.** Consider $J=3$ studies on $K=3$ treatments $\{1,2,3\}$ (reference
$1$): study $1$ is IPD on $\{1,2\}$, study $2$ is AgD on $\{1,3\}$, study $3$ is AgD on $\{2,3\}$, with a
single covariate ($p=1$) and shared EM. List the free parameters and their count, draw the treatment
graph and verify connectivity, and walk through blocks (i) to (iii) of @thm-mlnmr-identifiability-large to
confirm that every parameter is identified. Which single arm supplies the shared interaction
$\boldsymbol\beta_2$, and why must it be the IPD arm?
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-sema-gap}
**($\star$) Challenge (derivation). A closed form for the non-collapsibility gap.** For a single binary effect modifier
$X\in\{0,1\}$ with $\Pr(X=1)=q$, the logit link, and SEMA, derive a closed-form expression for the
$A$-versus-$B$ non-collapsibility gap
$\Delta^{\mathrm{Cond}}_{BA}-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})=(\gamma_A-\gamma_B)-\Delta_{BA}(\mathcal P^{*})$
in terms of $\mu_{*},\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2,\gamma_A,\gamma_B,q$. Prove that the gap is zero
when $q\in\{0,1\}$ (a degenerate covariate) and when $\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2=0$ (no spread
in the active-arm linear predictors), in agreement with @thm-aggregation-bias, and confirm your formula
reproduces the value $0.022502$ at the inputs of @exm-mlnmr-new-target. Discuss why the gap, unlike the
conditional contrast, cannot be eliminated by SEMA.
:::

::: {#exr-mlnmr-stc-reduction}
**($\star$) Proof. The STC reduction in detail.** Fix a logistic outcome family. Write the marginal STC predicted
arm means (Chapter 19) for an IPD trial on $\{A,C\}$ standardized to a comparator covariate distribution
$f_{BC}$, and the ML-NMR aggregate arm means @eq-mlnmr-est-aggmean over the same $f_{BC}$ using the same
fitted linear predictor. Prove the two are identical as functionals, and identify precisely the two ways
in which a full ML-NMR fit differs from this restriction: namely, that ML-NMR's likelihood incorporates
the AgD *outcomes* through @thm-aggregation, and that ML-NMR's estimand @thm-target-population-integral
admits any target population. Conclude that STC is the special case of ML-NMR obtained by fitting the
outcome surface on the IPD alone and fixing the target to the comparator, and state, with reference to
@thm-stc-consistency and the no-extrapolation theorem of Chapter 18, one situation in which the extra
information ML-NMR uses changes the answer and one in which it does not.
:::
